claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in the native state.
claims.source: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in the native (Doose et al., 2009; Ries et al., 2014; Neuweiler et al., 2009), unfolded (Sherman and Haran, 2011; Daidone et al., 2010) and intermediate states (Neuweiler et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in the unfolded state.
claims.source: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in the native (Doose et al., 2009; Ries et al., 2014; Neuweiler et al., 2009), unfolded (Sherman and Haran, 2011; Daidone et al., 2010) and intermediate states (Neuweiler et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in intermediate states.
claims.source: PET-FCS has been used extensively to measure the dynamics of proteins in the native (Doose et al., 2009; Ries et al., 2014; Neuweiler et al., 2009), unfolded (Sherman and Haran, 2011; Daidone et al., 2010) and intermediate states (Neuweiler et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Conformational dynamics across helices α1 and α3, and across helices α2 and α3, were monitored separately in two mutant variants of the protein designed for PET-FCS measurements.
claims.source: Conformational dynamics across helices α1 and α3, and across helices α2 and α3, were monitored separately in two mutant variants of the protein designed for PET-FCS measurements (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design, with reference to Figure 1.

claims.claim: Quenching of an Atto 655 moiety by a suitably placed Trp residue occurs when the two come within contact quenching distance (<1 nm).
claims.source: In each mutant variant, the dynamics leading to the quenching of an Atto 655 moiety introduced into the protein, by a suitably placed Trp residue, when the two come within contact quenching distance (<1 nm) (Vaiana et al., 2003), was measured as fluctuations in the Atto 655 fluorescence.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Autocorrelation functions (ACFs) for both the distances show three exponential processes, arising from sub-millisecond dynamics in the protein.
claims.source: Autocorrelation functions (ACFs) for both the distances show three exponential processes, arising from sub-millisecond dynamics in the protein.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the PET-FCS experiments.

claims.claim: The slow exponential process was found to represent the dynamics of folding from the U state to an intermediate state (I), by comparing the kinetics obtained from PET-FCS to the kinetics of folding of the Atto 655-labeled protein.
claims.source: The slow exponential process was found to represent the dynamics of folding from the U state to an intermediate state (I), by comparing the kinetics obtained from PET-FCS to the kinetics of folding of the Atto 655-labeled protein.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of PET-FCS data with microsecond mixing experiments.

claims.claim: The two faster exponential processes could be attributed to fluctuations in the native state.
claims.source: The two faster exponential processes could be attributed to fluctuations in the native state.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: The native state dynamics of moPrP result in global unfolding via an intermediate.
claims.source: Overall, it is shown that the native state dynamics of moPrP result in global unfolding via an intermediate.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Labeling with Atto 655 did not result in any alteration in the secondary structure of the protein, as indicated by the far-UV circular dichroism measurements.
claims.source: Labeling with Atto 655 did not result in any alteration in the secondary structure of the protein, as indicated by the far-UV circular dichroism measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: PET quenching occurs primarily by a static quenching mechanism.
claims.source: It is known that such quenching occurs primarily by a static quenching mechanism (Sauer and Neuweiler, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: PET from the Trp side-chain occurs within a few picoseconds.
claims.source: Since PET occurs within a few picoseconds (Lakowicz, 1999; Zhong and Zewail, 2001; Doose et al., 2005)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The observed rate constant of the overall quenching reaction reflects the rate constant for the formation of the dye-Trp complex.
claims.source: Since PET occurs within a few picoseconds (Lakowicz, 1999; Zhong and Zewail, 2001; Doose et al., 2005), and because dissociation of the dye-Trp complex is much slower (Sherman and Haran, 2011; Soranno et al., 2017), the observed rate constant of the overall quenching reaction reflects the rate constant for the formation of the dye-Trp complex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetics of PET and complex dissociation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The quenching distance, above which electron transfer cannot occur, is about 0.5 nm.
claims.source: However, in PET, the probability of electron transfer decreases asymptotically to near zero within less than a nanometer of separation; and the quenching distance, above which electron transfer cannot occur, is about 0.5 nm (Lewis et al., 1997; Vaiana et al., 2003)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The ACFs of both W144/C199-Atto moPrP and W171/C225-Atto moPrP showed three exponential components, in addition to the diffusion component.
claims.source: The ACFs of both W144/C199-Atto moPrP and W171/C225-Atto moPrP, showed three exponential components, in addition to the diffusion component (Figure 2a,b).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the PET-FCS experiments, shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The total amplitude of the exponential components for W144-C199-Atto moPrP was higher than that observed for W171/C225-Atto moPrP.
claims.source: The total amplitude of the exponential components for W144-C199-Atto moPrP was higher than that observed for W171/C225-Atto moPrP.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of experimental results from the two constructs.

claims.claim: The time constants and amplitudes of the exponential processes were found to be independent of the excitation power used in the FCS experiments.
claims.source: The time constants and amplitudes of the exponential processes were found to be independent of the excitation power used in the FCS experiments (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a control experiment result, documented in Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: The Trp-less control proteins showed negligible exponential components, confirming that these components originate from the quenching of the fluorescence of the Atto moiety attached to the protein by the Trp residue in the Trp-containing proteins.
claims.source: The Trp-less control proteins showed negligible exponential components, confirming that these components originate from the quenching of the fluorescence of the Atto moiety attached to the protein by the Trp residue in the Trp-containing proteins (Figure 2a,b).
claims.evidence: This is a control experiment result shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The hydrodynamic radius calculated from the diffusion coefficient obtained from the PET-FCS measurements was 2.8 nm, which matches well with the RH measured by dynamic light scattering experiments in earlier studies.
claims.source: The hydrodynamic radius calculated from the diffusion coefficient obtained from the PET-FCS measurements was 2.8 nm, which matches well with the RH measured by dynamic light scattering experiments in earlier studies (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim compares current measurements with previous DLS data, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The relative fluorescence intensity of the Trp-containing protein compared to Trp-less PET construct directly gives the fraction of molecules in the native state ensemble, in which the Atto 655 fluorescence is not quenched by PET from a Trp side-chain.
claims.source: With the assumption that the quenched states are completely non-fluorescent, the relative fluorescence intensity of the Trp-containing protein compared to Trp-less PET construct directly gives the fraction of molecules in the native state ensemble, in which the Atto 655 fluorescence is not quenched by PET from a Trp side-chain.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on an assumption about the quenched states.

claims.claim: Conformational fluctuations on the 0.5–20 µs time scale have been observed in the native state ensembles of other proteins.
claims.source: Conformational fluctuations on this time scale have been observed in the native state ensembles of other proteins (Jensen et al., 2011; Ries et al., 2014; Schulze et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The unfolding of W144/C199-Atto moPrP occurred in a single kinetic phase that accounted for the entire equilibrium unfolding amplitude of unfolding.
claims.source: The unfolding of W144/C199-Atto moPrP occurred in a single kinetic phase (Figure 3a) that accounted for the entire equilibrium unfolding amplitude of unfolding (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from microsecond mixing experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Extrapolation of the denaturant dependence of the unfolding rate constant to zero urea concentration predicted an apparent unfolding rate constant of about 400 s−1 in native conditions.
claims.source: Extrapolation of the denaturant dependence of the unfolding rate constant to zero urea concentration, predicted an apparent unfolding rate constant of about 400 s−1 in native conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an extrapolation from experimental data.

claims.claim: The refolding of W144/C199-Atto moPrP occurred in two kinetic phases whose total amplitude accounted for the entire equilibrium amplitude of folding.
claims.source: The refolding of W144/C199-Atto moPrP occurred in two kinetic phases (Figure 3b), whose total amplitude accounted for the entire equilibrium amplitude of folding (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from microsecond mixing experiments shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The simplest explanation for the observation of two kinetic phases is that folding occurs via an U↔ I ↔ N mechanism, in which I is a folding intermediate.
claims.source: The simplest explanation for the observation of two kinetic phases is that folding occurs via an U↔ I ↔ N mechanism, in which I is a folding intermediate.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the kinetic data.

claims.claim: The slow kinetic phase had a rate constant of ~500 s−1 and accounted for about 33% of the total amplitude of the decrease in fluorescence seen for folding from U to N.
claims.source: The slow kinetic phase had a rate constant of ~500 s−1 (Figure 3d), and accounted for about 33% of the total amplitude of the decrease in fluorescence seen for folding from U to N.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the kinetic experiments shown in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: The dependence on denaturant concentration of the rate constant of the fast phase observed in the microsecond mixing experiments extrapolates into the dependence on denaturant concentration of the rate constant of the slower exponential process observed in the PET-FCS measurements.
claims.source: Figure 3d shows that the dependence on denaturant concentration of the rate constant of the fast phase observed in the microsecond mixing experiments, extrapolates into the dependence on denaturant concentration of the rate constant of the slower exponential process observed in the PET-FCS measurements.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing data in Figure 3d.

claims.claim: The rate constant of the slow exponential process measured in 0.75 M urea by PET-FCS matches the fast rate constant of folding in 0.75 M urea.
claims.source: It is also seen that the rate constant of the slow exponential process measured in 0.75 M urea by PET-FCS, matches the fast rate constant of folding in 0.75 M urea.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of rate constants from different experimental methods.

claims.claim: The observation that the rate constant of the fast phase of folding observed in the microsecond mixing experiments was identical with the rate constant of the slow exponential process seen in the PET-FCS experiments indicated that the same transition was being monitored in both measurements.
claims.source: The observation that the rate constant of the fast phase of folding observed in the microsecond mixing experiments was identical with the rate constant of the slow exponential process seen in the PET-FCS experiments, indicated that the same transition was being monitored in both measurements.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of rate constants from two different methods.

claims.claim: The slowest exponential process seen in the PET-FCS experiments represents a conformational fluctuation of the unfolded state at low concentrations of urea, which is not a random fluctuation, but which leads to the formation of a productive folding intermediate.
claims.source: It is important to note that the slowest exponential process seen in the PET-FCS experiments, represents a conformational fluctuation of the unfolded state at low concentrations of urea, which is not a random fluctuation, but which leads to the formation of a productive folding intermediate.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the PET-FCS data in the context of folding.

claims.claim: Salt is known to trigger the aggregation of moPrP at pH 4.
claims.source: Salt is known to trigger the aggregation of moPrP at pH 4 (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2010; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2016; Sengupta and Udgaonkar, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: In the presence of salt, the combined amplitude (K1 +K2) of the two faster exponential processes was found to have slightly increased for W171/C225-Atto moPrP.
claims.source: In the presence of salt, the combined amplitude (K1 +K2) of the two faster exponential processes was found to have slightly increased for W171/C225-Atto moPrP (Figure 5a,b).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from PET-FCS experiments with salt, shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: The time scale of the native state fluctuations was observed to become faster upon the addition of salt.
claims.source: The time scale of the native state fluctuations was observed to become faster upon the addition of salt (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from PET-FCS experiments with salt, documented in Table 1.

claims.claim: Equilibrium unfolding experiments carried out at pH four for W144/C199-Atto moPrP in the presence of salt indicated that the protein is destabilized by approximately 0.7 kcal/mol upon addition of salt.
claims.source: Equilibrium unfolding experiments carried out at pH four for W144/C199-Atto moPrP in the presence of salt indicated that the protein is destabilized by approximately 0.7 kcal/mol upon addition of salt (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: Both the amplitude and the time constant of the slowest exponential process was seen to decrease upon the addition of salt, at pH 4, for both the PET pairs.
claims.source: Both the amplitude and the time constant of the slowest exponential process was seen to decrease upon the addition of salt, at pH 4, for both the PET pairs (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from PET-FCS experiments with salt, documented in Table 1.

claims.claim: The rate constant of the N → N** transition measured for the α2-α3 segment by monitoring fluctuations in W171/C225-Atto moPrP was nearly an order of magnitude slower than that measured for the α1-α3 segment, by monitoring fluctuations in W144/C199-Atto moPrP.
claims.source: It was observed that the rate constant of the N → N** transition measured for the α2-α3 segment by monitoring fluctuations in W171/C225-Atto moPrP, was nearly an order of magnitude slower than that measured for the α1-α3 segment, by monitoring fluctuations in W144/C199-Atto moPrP (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of rate constants from the two constructs, shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: The addition of salt had a significant effect on the rate constants of both the N → N** and N** → N transitions measured for the α2-α3 segment, but had a negligible effect on the rate constants measured for the α1-α3 segment.
claims.source: The addition of salt had a significant effect on the rate constants of both the N → N** and N** → N transitions measured for the α2-α3 segment, but had a negligible effect on the rate constants measured for the α1-α3 segment (Figure 6b).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the effects of salt on the two constructs, shown in Figure 6b.

claims.claim: A recent real-time NMR monitored aggregation study of moPrP has shown that the addition of salt causes the disruption of the salt bridge between residues K193 and E195, which triggers the aggregation process.
claims.source: A recent real-time NMR monitored aggregation study of moPrP, has shown that the addition of salt causes the disruption of the salt bridge between residues K193 and E195, which triggers the aggregation process (Sengupta and Udgaonkar, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Earlier studies have indicated that the dynamics in the U state of prion protein play a role in initiating misfolding and oligomerisation.
claims.source: Earlier studies have indicated that the dynamics in the U state of prion protein play a role in initiating misfolding and oligomerisation (Yu et al., 2012; Srivastava and Lapidus, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: In the current study it was shown that the fluctuations within the N state of the protein are responsible for the misfolding of the moPrP.
claims.source: In the current study it was shown that the fluctuations within the N state of the protein are responsible for the misfolding of the moPrP.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results of the current study.

claims.claim: For several proteins, aggregation has been shown to proceed from partially folded intermediates on protein folding/unfolding pathways.
claims.source: In the case of several proteins, aggregation has been shown to proceed from partially folded intermediates on protein folding/unfolding pathways (Fink, 1998; Hamid Wani and Udgaonkar, 2006; Jahn and Parker, 2006; De Simone et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Upon the addition of salt, N is destabilized by 0.7 kcal/mol.

claims.claim: I is destabilized less, by 0.4 kcal/mol with respect to the U state upon the addition of salt.

claims.claim: Force spectroscopy studies of the Syrian hamster prion protein (SHaPrP) had suggested that the U state sampled three off-pathway compact intermediates.
claims.source: Force spectroscopy studies of the Syrian hamster prion protein (SHaPrP), had suggested that the U state sampled three off-pathway compact intermediates (Yu et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The occupancy of some of the off-pathway compact intermediates was more for a disease-linked mutant variant of the protein.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Disruption of the disulphide bond in the prion protein leads to its unfolding to a molten globule form.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Several other studies have shown that SHaPrP (90-231) is natively structured at acidic pH.
claims.source: In that study, the data appeared to suggest that the fluctuations might arise from the U state, but that could not have been the case because several other studies have shown that SHaPrP (90-231) is natively structured at acidic pH (Bjorndahl et al., 2011; Donne et al., 1997), including at pH 4 (Khan et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The study of the native state dynamics of moPrP, across the α1-α3 and α2-α3 segments, monitored by the PET-FCS methodology, reveals three distinct processes, well-separated in time.
claims.source: The study of the native state dynamics of moPrP, across the α1-α3 and α2-α3 segments, monitored by the PET-FCS methodology, using carefully designed single-free cysteine and single-tryptophan-containing variants, reveals three distinct processes, well-separated in time.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the PET-FCS experiments.

claims.claim: The faster processes (~0.5–20 μs time constants) represent dynamics within the native state ensemble leading to the formation of the non-fluorescent complexes N* and N**.
claims.source: The faster processes (~0.5–20 μs time constants) represent dynamics within the native state ensemble leading to the formation of the non-fluorescent complexes N* and N**.

claims.claim: The slow process (50–100 μs time constant) reports on the U ↔ I transition of folding.

claims.claim: The rate constant of the N →N** transition, in the absence of salt, is an order of magnitude slower when measured by monitoring fluctuations across α2-α3, than for the fluctuations across α1-α3, possibly because the fluctuations across α2-α3 are slowed down by the disulphide bond, packing interactions and salt bridges in the core of the protein.

claims.claim: The folding landscape and the fluctuations within the native state ensemble are modulated by salt.
claims.source: The folding landscape and the fluctuations within the native state ensemble are modulated by salt (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the salt-dependent experiments, illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The addition of salt results in an increase in the rate constants of both the N → N** and N** → N transitions, possibly because critical ionic interactions are lost.

claims.claim: The enhancement of the time scale of native state fluctuations upon the addition of salt suggest that these fluctuations play a role in the initiation of misfolding of the protein.

results.result: The authors designed two PET-FCS constructs (W144/C199-Atto and W171/C225-Atto moPrP) to monitor conformational dynamics across different helical segments of the full-length mouse prion protein under native conditions. CD spectroscopy confirmed that Atto 655 labeling did not alter the secondary structure of the protein.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C27, C79, C80 describe the experimental design and constructs used, which are clearly documented with structural details and figures. Claim C33 provides control data (CD spectroscopy) confirming that the labeling procedure did not perturb protein structure. The experimental approach is well-justified and appropriately controlled.

results.result: PET-FCS measurements revealed three exponential processes in the autocorrelation functions for both constructs, in addition to the diffusion component. These exponential components were independent of excitation power and were absent in Trp-less control proteins, confirming they arise from PET quenching.
results.evaluation: Claims C29 and C38 report the primary observation of three exponential processes. Claims C81, C40, and C41 provide critical controls: good fit quality (residuals), power independence, and Trp-less controls. These controls effectively rule out artifacts and confirm the PET origin of the signals. The data quality and controls are appropriate.

results.result: The slowest exponential process observed by PET-FCS (50-100 μs) represents the U ↔ I transition during protein folding. This assignment was validated by microsecond mixing experiments showing biphasic refolding kinetics, with the fast phase rate constant matching the slow PET-FCS component.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C52, C53, and C74 assign the slow PET-FCS component to the U↔I transition. This is strongly supported by microsecond mixing data (C45, C47-C51) showing that rate constants from the two independent methods converge (C50, C51). The chevron plot extrapolation (C50) and rate constant matching at 0.75 M urea (C51) provide compelling evidence. The interpretation is logically sound and experimentally validated.

results.result: The two faster exponential processes (0.5-20 μs) observed by PET-FCS were attributed to fluctuations within the native state ensemble, leading to formation of non-fluorescent states N* and N**. This assignment was supported by agreement between equilibrium constants calculated from fluorescence spectra and PET-FCS amplitudes.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C73, and C4 assign the fast components to native state fluctuations. Claims C100 and C101 provide key validation: K1+K2 values calculated independently from fluorescence spectra and PET-FCS data agree well (Table 2). Claim C43 explains the underlying assumption. The convergence of independent measurements strengthens the interpretation, though the assumption of complete quenching (C43) introduces some uncertainty.

results.result: Addition of 150 mM NaCl enhanced the time scale of native state fluctuations in the protein core, particularly affecting the α2-α3 segment. Salt destabilized the native state by ~0.7 kcal/mol and increased rate constants for N↔N** transitions in the α2-α3 region, suggesting these fluctuations play a role in initiating protein misfolding.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 document the effects of salt on PET-FCS parameters, showing faster fluctuations and altered amplitudes. Claim C57 provides thermodynamic data on salt-induced destabilization. Claims C59-C60 show differential effects on the two constructs, with α2-α3 being more affected. Claims C76-C78 and C116 draw conclusions about the role in misfolding. The data are internally consistent and the salt effects are well-documented, though the mechanistic link to aggregation (C78) is somewhat inferential.

results.result: The authors conclude that native state dynamics of moPrP result in global unfolding via an intermediate, and that fluctuations within the native state lead to sampling of aggregation-competent conformations. Both the intermediate I and native-like states N* and N** are proposed to be important in initiating misfolding and aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C32, C6, C63, C117, and C122 represent major conclusions about the role of native state dynamics in aggregation. While the PET-FCS and salt data support enhanced fluctuations under aggregation-promoting conditions, direct evidence linking the observed conformational states (N*, N**, I) to actual aggregation is limited. The connection relies heavily on correlation (salt promotes both faster fluctuations and aggregation) rather than direct demonstration that these states are aggregation precursors. Additional experiments directly monitoring aggregation from these states would strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: Salt differentially destabilizes the native state (0.7 kcal/mol) and intermediate I (0.4 kcal/mol), increasing the relative population of I. The U↔I transition is rapid and I is positioned on the unfolding side of the major free energy barrier. The authors suggest I might play a direct role in misfolding.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 provide thermodynamic measurements from equilibrium unfolding experiments (Table 3, Figure 7). Claims C119-C120 interpret the kinetic and thermodynamic data to position I on the energy landscape. Claim C95 notes that salt-perturbed interactions are present in I, supporting its on-pathway nature. Claim C121 is more speculative but reasonably supported by the correlation between I population and aggregation propensity. The thermodynamic analysis is sound, though the direct role in misfolding (C121) remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The rate constant for the N→N** transition in the α2-α3 segment is an order of magnitude slower than in the α1-α3 segment, possibly due to constraints from the disulfide bond, packing interactions, and salt bridges in the protein core. The α1-β1-β2 subdomain is attached through a flexible loop allowing more rapid fluctuations.
results.evaluation: Claim C59 reports the experimental observation of different rate constants between constructs (Figure 6a). Claims C75 and C113 provide structural explanations for this difference. The observation is clear from the data, and the structural rationalization is reasonable given the known architecture of the prion protein. The explanation is speculative but well-grounded in structural knowledge.

results.result: Salt had a significant effect on rate constants for the α2-α3 segment but negligible effect on the α1-α3 segment. This is attributed to salt-induced disruption of the K193-E195 salt bridge, which increases flexibility and enhances helix separation rates in the α2-α3 core region.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 reports the differential salt effects (Figure 6b). Claim C61 cites NMR evidence for salt bridge disruption. Claims C114-C115 provide mechanistic explanations. The experimental observation is clear, and the mechanistic explanation is supported by independent NMR data from prior work. The interpretation is reasonable though somewhat speculative.

results.result: The hydrodynamic radius calculated from PET-FCS diffusion coefficients (2.8 nm) matches previous DLS measurements, and the experimentally determined diffusion coefficient was 90±10 μm²/s. Diffusion times for the labeled proteins were ~300 μs, confirming monomeric protein at the concentrations used.
results.evaluation: Claims C42 and C131 report measurements that validate the protein is monomeric and not aggregated under experimental conditions. Claims C82-C84 provide specific diffusion time measurements. The agreement with prior DLS data (C42) and the consistency of measurements across constructs support the quality of the data and confirm that aggregation is not occurring during measurements.

results.result: Equilibrium unfolding experiments showed 4-fold and 2-fold fluorescence enhancement upon unfolding for W144/C199-Atto and W171/C225-Atto moPrP, respectively. This increase is explained by release of PET quenching that occurs in the native state. In 6 M urea, PET-FCS amplitudes were >10-fold lower than in native conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 report equilibrium unfolding data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). Claim C87 provides the interpretation. Claim C88 shows that PET quenching is suppressed at high denaturant. These observations are internally consistent and support the model that quenching occurs in the native state. The data quality appears good and the interpretation is straightforward.

results.result: Thermodynamic parameters from equilibrium unfolding experiments yielded ΔG_NU values of 3.9 and 3.6 kcal/mol for W144/C199-Atto and W171/C225-Atto moPrP, respectively, with m-values of 1.3 and 1.7 kcal/mol/M.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 report thermodynamic parameters obtained from fitting equilibrium unfolding data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). The values are reasonable for a protein of this size and the m-values are within expected ranges. The data appear to be properly analyzed using standard two-state fitting procedures.

results.result: The free energy barriers between N and N*/N** are much smaller than the barrier between N and I. Consequently, N* and N** will be sampled much more frequently than I via fluctuations within the native state ensemble.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 interpret the energy landscape based on the observed time scales and amplitudes. The inference is logical: faster processes (0.5-20 μs for N↔N*/N**) versus slower process (50-100 μs for U↔I) imply lower barriers for the native state fluctuations. This is consistent with the free energy diagram (Figure 7) and represents a reasonable interpretation of the kinetic data.

results.result: Extrapolation of unfolding rate constants to zero urea predicted an apparent unfolding rate constant of ~400 s⁻¹ under native conditions. Control experiments showed the fast folding phase rate constant was independent of flow rate, and PET quenching efficiency was unaffected by urea up to 0.75 M.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 reports the extrapolated unfolding rate. Claims C93, C96, and C97 describe important controls ruling out artifacts from mixing or denaturant effects on PET efficiency. These controls are appropriate and strengthen confidence in the kinetic measurements. The extrapolation appears reasonable based on the chevron plot (Figure 3d).

results.result: The authors compare their results to previous force spectroscopy and Trp-Cys quenching studies on Syrian hamster prion protein, noting important differences in protein constructs (full-length vs truncated, intact vs disrupted disulfide bond) and arguing that aggregation-linked fluctuations likely arise from the native state rather than solely from the unfolded state.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 and C125-C130 discuss prior work and highlight experimental differences that could explain discrepancies. The authors correctly note that the SHaPrP used in force spectroscopy had a disrupted disulfide bond (C70, C126), which would significantly alter the protein's behavior. Claims C71, C128 cite evidence that SHaPrP is natively folded at acidic pH, supporting the argument in C129-C130 that native state fluctuations are important. The comparison is fair and the distinctions are scientifically valid.
